docs.title: Home
docs.text:
RISICO

RISICO (Rischio Incendi E Coordinamento) is the wildfire danger forecasting model developed by CIMA Research Foundation and used operationally by the Italian Civil Protection. This Rust implementation runs RISICO, the Canadian Fire Weather Index and eight more fire danger indices on gridded weather forecasts, from a single cell up to continental domains.

Try it in your browser Get started CLI usage Developer guide API reference

docs.title: What's included
docs.text:
• The RISICO model: dead fine fuel moisture, rate of spread and fireline intensity on every cell, driven by temperature, humidity, wind, rain and snow cover, with vegetation, slope and aspect from static layers.
  • More indices from the same inputs: the Canadian FWI System, Keetch–Byram, McArthur Mark 5, Angström, Fosberg, Nesterov, Sharples, Orieux and Hot–Dry–Windy (see Fire danger indices).
  • A streaming runner: every model is processed in spatial tiles, timestamp by timestamp, so memory stays bounded however large the domain (Tiled streaming execution).
  • Pure-Rust I/O: NetCDF and legacy zbin inputs, NetCDF / GeoTIFF / Zarr / PNG outputs, GeoTIFF static data and NetCDF warm state, with no native C libraries.
  • A Rust library: the models without the runner, to embed in other programs (Programmatic workflow, API reference).
  • A WebAssembly build: the same binary compiled for wasm32-wasip1, which powers the interactive demo.

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
1. Prepare the static data as aligned GeoTIFF layers: a domain mask, slope, aspect and vegetation (see Configuration).
  2. Write a configuration.yml listing the models, their warm-state directory and their outputs.
  3. Run risico-2023 <run date> configuration.yml <input> on a directory of NetCDF weather inputs (or a list of legacy zbin files).
  4. Read the NetCDF (or GeoTIFF, Zarr, PNG) outputs; the warm state written at the configured hour seeds the next day's run.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
The API reference is generated from the source with rustdoc and published with this site:

Open the API reference

It documents the risico library crate, the models without the runner. Start from the crate page: it explains the concepts and units, with a tested example. The main modules:

Module Contents risico::models::input Input, InputElement: the weather of one timestamp; InputVariableName: the variable names of input files risico::models::output Output, OutputElement, OutputVariableName: the output variables of every model risico::modules::risico RISICO: properties, vegetation, warm state, state, the legacy / v2023 / v2025 formulations risico::modules::fwi Canadian FWI System: properties, warm state, state, the legacy / cffdrs / sliding_window formulations risico::modules All models: KBDI, Mark 5, Angström, Fosberg, Nesterov, Sharples, Orieux, HDW risico::config The configuration.yml schema (feature config) risico::constants Shared constants, among them NODATAVAL

To build it locally:

cargo doc --no-deps --lib --open

For a guided tour with complete programs see the Programmatic Workflow.

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
The repository builds four commands:

Command Purpose risico-2023 Run the models of a configuration on a set of weather inputs streaming-inspect Validate a configuration and print its tile plan, without running static-converter Convert legacy RISICO/FWI cell files to GeoTIFF static layers warm-state-converter Convert legacy warm-state files to NetCDF snapshots 
cargo build --release --bins
ls target/release/{risico-2023,streaming-inspect,static-converter,warm-state-converter}

Every command prints its usage with --help.

docs.title: risico-2023
docs.text:
Usage: risico-2023 <DATE> <CONFIG_PATH> <INPUT_PATH>

Arguments:
  <DATE>         Model date in the format YYYYMMDDHHMM
  <CONFIG_PATH>  Path to the configuration file
  <INPUT_PATH>   Path to the input data file

Options:
  -h, --help     Print help
  -V, --version  Print version

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: DATE The run date, in UTC. Each model loads the newest warm-state snapshot at or before it (within max_age_hours) and starts from there. The weather inputs must start after it. CONFIG_PATH A YAML configuration: the models to run, their static data, warm state and outputs (see Configuration). INPUT_PATH Either a directory of NetCDF weather files (every .nc file in it is read, see Getting Started) or a text file listing legacy .zbin files, one per line.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
./target/release/risico-2023 \
  202607010000 \
  /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  /data/weather/20260701/

A run reads the static data and warm state of every model, then streams the inputs one timestamp at a time through each tile of each model, writing outputs at the configured hours and the warm state at warm_state_hour (see Tiled Streaming Execution).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect RUST_LOG info Log level: error, warn, info, debug, trace. Logs go to standard error. TMPDIR /tmp Base of the scratch directory when the configuration sets none.

The command exits with a non-zero status and an error message when the configuration, the static data or the inputs cannot be read.

docs.title: streaming-inspect
docs.text:
Checks a configuration without reading any weather: it loads the static data, resolves every model and prints the tile plan the runner would use. Useful before deploying a new configuration, or to try other tile sizes.

Usage: streaming-inspect [OPTIONS] <DATE> <CONFIG>

Arguments:
  <DATE>    Model date in YYYYMMDDHHMM form
  <CONFIG>  YAML or legacy text configuration

Options:
      --tile-height <TILE_HEIGHT>        Override raster tile height
      --tile-width <TILE_WIDTH>          Override raster tile width
      --cells-per-tile <CELLS_PER_TILE>  Override legacy cells per tile

./target/release/streaming-inspect 202607010000 configuration.yml --tile-height 256 --tile-width 256

docs.title: static-converter
docs.text:
Converts the legacy regular-grid static files to the aligned GeoTIFF layers the model reads (see Converting Legacy Data).

Usage: static-converter risico [OPTIONS] --cells <CELLS> --grid <GRID> --output <OUTPUT>
      --cells <CELLS>    RISICO cell file: lon lat slope aspect vegetation
      --grid <GRID>      Legacy grid file (GRIDNROWS=, MINLAT=, ...)
      --output <OUTPUT>  Destination directory for the GeoTIFF layers
      --ppf <PPF>        Optional legacy two-column summer/winter PPF file

Usage: static-converter fwi --cells <CELLS> --grid <GRID> --output <OUTPUT>
      --cells <CELLS>    FWI cell file: lon lat
      --grid <GRID>      Legacy grid file
      --output <OUTPUT>  Destination directory for the domain mask

docs.title: warm-state-converter
docs.text:
Converts legacy text warm states to NetCDF snapshots, validated against a domain mask.

Usage: warm-state-converter config [OPTIONS] --config <CONFIG> --model-name <MODEL_NAME> --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>
      --config <CONFIG>                Migrated YAML configuration containing GeoTIFF and NetCDF warm-state settings
      --model-name <MODEL_NAME>        `model_name` of the model entry to convert, as it appears in the config file
      --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>  Legacy filename prefix, or a directory when files are named only by timestamp
      --latest-only                    Convert only the newest legacy snapshot
      --overwrite                      Replace an existing NetCDF snapshot with the same timestamp

Usage: warm-state-converter risico|fwi [OPTIONS] --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX> --domain-mask <DOMAIN_MASK> --output <OUTPUT> --model-version <MODEL_VERSION>
      --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>  Legacy filename prefix, or a directory when files are named only by timestamp
      --domain-mask <DOMAIN_MASK>      GeoTIFF domain mask used to validate cell count and define the output grid
      --output <OUTPUT>                Destination directory for NetCDF snapshots
      --model-version <MODEL_VERSION>  Model version stored in and validated against each snapshot
      --latest-only                    Convert only the newest legacy snapshot
      --overwrite                      Replace an existing NetCDF snapshot with the same timestamp

The config form takes paths and model metadata from a configuration that already points at the GeoTIFF static data and the NetCDF warm-state directory; the risico and fwi forms take them explicitly.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
RISICO and FWI configure their static data and warm state as aligned, single-band GeoTIFF layers and NetCDF snapshots. This is the only supported layout: the older cell/PPF/vegetation-ID text files and plain-text warm-state files are no longer readable directly by the model binary, and configuration files must be YAML (the older whole-file .txt key/value format is no longer supported). Existing deployments convert once with static-converter and warm-state-converter (see Converting legacy data) before switching their configuration over.

models:
  - type: RISICO
    model_name: RISICO2023
    model_version: v2025
    static_data:
      type: geotiff
      domain_mask: /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif
      slope: /opt/risico/static/slope.tif
      aspect: /opt/risico/static/aspect.tif
      vegetation_id: /opt/risico/static/vegetation_id.tif
      vegetation_catalog: /opt/risico/static/p_vegetazione.csv
      ppf_summer: null
      ppf_winter: null
    warm_state:
      type: netcdf
      directory: /opt/risico/state-nc
      max_age_hours: 120
      on_missing: error
    warm_state_hour: 0
    output_time_resolution: 1
    output_types: []

The domain mask defines the grid and active cells. All layers must be north-up, unrotated EPSG:4326 rasters with identical dimensions and affine transforms. Slope and aspect are stored in degrees. A non-zero, non-nodata mask pixel is active. PPF layers must either both be configured or both omitted.

NetCDF snapshots store every state field as a georeferenced y, x grid. The files include longitude and latitude coordinate axes, EPSG and affine-transform metadata, and fill values outside the active domain. On load, state is sampled onto the configured domain with nearest-neighbour sampling, so a snapshot can survive a compatible grid-resolution change. A target active cell that maps outside the snapshot or onto a fill pixel makes that snapshot invalid. Snapshots are also validated against the model version, written through a temporary file, and atomically renamed. A run with no valid NetCDF snapshot follows on_missing directly: defaults seeds the run with default state, error stops the run. There is no automatic fallback to a legacy text state; convert existing legacy warm state once with warm-state-converter (below) before switching a deployment over.

FWI uses the same domain-mask and warm-state configuration, without the RISICO-specific layers:

models:
  - type: FWI
    model_name: FWIWORLD
    model_version: legacy
    static_data:
      type: geotiff
      domain_mask: /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif
    warm_state:
      type: netcdf
      directory: /opt/risico/state-nc
      max_age_hours: 120
      on_missing: error
    warm_state_hour: 0
    output_types: []

FWI model versions:

  • cffdrs: the canonical daily Canadian FWI System (Van Wagner 1987; equations and constants of the cffdrs R package, src/lib/modules/fwi/cffdrs.rs, tested against its published fixtures). The daily step runs at each cell's local standard noon (tzf-rs time zone, IANA rules, no DST), with temperature, humidity and wind interpolated linearly between the input steps around noon and the rain accumulated since the previous noon. The snapshot keeps the codes and the rain accumulated since the last noon, so a restart is exact. Write one map per day after the latest noon of the domain with output_time_resolution: 24 and output_time_offset (hours from the run date, e.g. 12 for domains whose standard offsets are all >= 0).
  • legacy: the port used by FWI-ITALIA-ICON/IFS (civil-time noon, daily step computed when the output is written; kept unchanged).
  • sliding_window: rolling 24 h windows.

FWI snapshots preserve each cell's complete moisture/rain history as history, y, x grids plus a history_count grid. Legacy-model snapshots use one scalar observation per pixel, matching the deployed rain ffmc dmc dc warm-state representation. The fallback reader accepts both the current five-column history text format and the deployed four-column scalar format.

Existing legacy snapshots can be converted before cutover: see Converting legacy data.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Each model lists its output_types: where to write, on which regular grid, in which format, and which variables (see Fire danger indices for the variable names of each model). Values are combined over the native cells of each output pixel with cluster_mode (Mean, Max, Min, ...) and rounded to a multiple of 10precision (-1 keeps one decimal).

    output_time_resolution: 1
    output_types:
      - internal_name: RISICO2023
        name: RISICO2023
        path: /opt/risico/output
        format: NETCDF
        compression_level: 7
        grid:
          nrows: 1200
          ncols: 1378
          min_lat: 35.139
          max_lat: 47.427
          min_lon: 5.975
          max_lon: 20.085
        variables:
          - internal_name: dffm
            name: UMB
            cluster_mode: Min
            precision: -1
          - internal_name: V
            name: V
            cluster_mode: Max
            precision: 0

The legacy grid_path (a GRIDNROWS= / MINLAT= text file) is still accepted in place of grid.

Output types are written as ZBIN, NETCDF, ZARR, PNGWJSON or GEOTIFF; any other format is a configuration error. ZARR writes one Zarr v3 store per variable (<path>/<name>.zarr) with the same time, latitude and longitude axes as the NetCDF output, one zstd-compressed chunk per timestamp, replacing any store left by an earlier run. Zarr stores take no global lock, so a timestamp's variables are compressed in parallel.

NETCDF output types accept a compression_level (0 to 9, default 7); for ZARR the same key is the zstd level (0 to 22). NetCDF-4 files are written by the in-repo nc4-stream crate (crates/nc4-stream), a pure-Rust streaming writer: each timestamp's grid is shuffled and deflated on the thread that produced it and appended to the file as one chunk, so the variables of a timestamp compress in parallel and an open output file costs one chunk of memory however long the timeline is. The chunk index and the rest of the file metadata are written when the run ends, so output files are readable only after a run finishes or fails cleanly. The files have the same structure netcdf-c writes (unlimited time, one chunk per timestamp, dimension scales), so ncdump, xarray and GDAL read them as before.

docs.title: Converting Legacy Data
docs.text:
Convert existing regular-grid static files with the offline static-converter utility, which writes single-band EPSG:4326 GeoTIFF layers. The converter detects, per axis, whether legacy bounds represent outer edges or cell centres; this accommodates the conventions used by the deployed grids.

cargo run --release --bin static-converter -- risico \
  --cells /share/risico/RISICO2023/STATIC/risico2023_input_1km.txt \
  --grid /share/risico/RISICO2023/GRID/input_1km_GRID.txt \
  --output /opt/risico/RISICO2023/STATIC/geotiff

cargo run --release --bin static-converter -- fwi \
  --cells /share/risico/FWIWORLD/STATIC/FWI_world.txt \
  --grid /share/risico/FWIWORLD/GRID/GRID.txt \
  --output /opt/risico/FWIWORLD/STATIC/geotiff

The converter checks that cells are unique and in the canonical north-to-south, west-to-east order. This keeps legacy state rows aligned during a progressive migration.

For warm-state-converter, --legacy-prefix may name a prefix or a directory whose files are bare YYYYMMDDHHMM timestamps. Every written snapshot is read back and validated before conversion is reported as successful. A malformed legacy file is reported without preventing other discovered snapshots from being checked.

docs.title: Warm state
docs.text:
Existing legacy snapshots can be converted before cutover. The domain mask defines the output NetCDF grid and places each text row at its corresponding active pixel. By default all timestamped files matching the prefix are converted; existing NetCDF files are skipped unless --overwrite is used.

cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- config \
  --config /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  --model-name RISICO2023 \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0RISICO_ \
  --latest-only

# The explicit form is useful outside a migrated deployment:
cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- risico \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0RISICO_ \
  --domain-mask /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif \
  --output /opt/risico/state-nc \
  --model-version v2025

cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- fwi \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0FWI_ \
  --domain-mask /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif \
  --output /opt/risico/state-nc \
  --model-version legacy \
  --latest-only

docs.title: Interactive Demo
docs.text:
The risico-2023 binary is compiled to WebAssembly (wasm32-wasip1) and runs entirely in your browser: no server, no upload. It is the same program as the operational build. The page writes its weather inputs as NetCDF files and its static layers as GeoTIFFs into an in-memory filesystem, runs the binary on them in a Web Worker, and reads back the NetCDF-4 files it writes.

Three levels, from a single cell to the whole country:

  1. One cell, your weather. Pick a cell on the map, set a weather scenario with the sliders and, if you like, change its vegetation, slope and aspect. Nothing is downloaded: all ten models run on one cell in well under a second.
  2. One cell, real weather. The same cell driven by real hourly weather: July 2025, bundled with the page as a NetCDF file, or today's analysis and forecast from Open-Meteo.
  3. Liguria at 1 km. RISICO and FWI on the 16 000 cells of a Liguria cut-out of the Italian domain, with the same choice of weather on a 0.125° grid. Browse the maps in time and click a cell for its series.

docs.title: 1 · One cell, your weather
docs.text:
Click any cell of the domain, a 1 km cut-out of the Italian one around Liguria: the panel shows its vegetation, slope and aspect from the static layers. Set a weather scenario (start date, length, mean temperature and daily range, humidity, wind, a rain event) and, if you like, override the vegetation class, slope and aspect. Run all indices runs the ten models on that cell.

The results come as interactive charts, grouped by model: the weather actually used, RISICO hourly (fine fuel moisture, rate of spread, intensity, wind and temperature effects), the FWI moisture codes and behaviour indices, and every other index.

docs.title: 2 · One cell, real weather
docs.text: The same cell with real hourly weather. By default the page uses its July 2025 sample, a NetCDF input bundled with the site, so nothing is requested from outside: pick the first day and the length of the period. Alternatively, Today requests the analysis of up to two months before now and up to ten days of forecast from Open-Meteo; a dashed line marks the current time.

docs.title: 3 · Liguria at 1 km
docs.text:
RISICO and FWI on every cell of the domain, on any period of the July 2025 sample (a week takes a few seconds) or on today's forecast. When the run ends, pick a variable and move through time with the slider; the legend uses the operational palettes.

Click a cell for its full series of the selected variable:

About this demo

The run is single-threaded, since wasm32 has no threads; the native build processes tiles in parallel. Every run starts from default moisture (on_missing: defaults) and spins up on the past days of weather. That is enough for the fine fuel moisture of RISICO, but slow codes such as the FWI drought code (DC) or KBDI need months to settle. Mark 5 and KBDI use a mean annual rainfall of 800 mm and Orieux a heat index of 70 for every cell.

The July 2025 sample comes from the Open-Meteo historical forecast archive and is served with the site; weather data by Open-Meteo.com, licensed under CC BY 4.0; the same files run with the command-line model, see Try it with the sample data. Today's weather is requested by your browser from Open-Meteo's free API: 2 m temperature and humidity, 10 m wind, precipitation and snow depth. The free tier allows about 600 locations a minute; the Liguria map needs about 200, and the page waits and retries if the limit is reached.

See Building the Web Demo for how the bundle is built.

docs.title: Tiled Streaming Execution
docs.text: Tiled streaming is the only production execution path. The former whole-domain run_* loops and the runtime enabled switch have been removed. The same runner is used by RISICO, FWI, Mark5, KBDI, Angstrom, Fosberg, Nesterov, Sharples, Orieux, and HDW.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
For each configured model, execution proceeds as follows:

  1. Build a spatial tile plan, gather every tile's immutable properties once, seed every tile's live state from the warm state, and register each tile's input coordinates. The whole-domain property and warm-state arrays are released at this point.
  2. Process the input timeline in timestamp order, decoding each timestamp's source fields once.
  3. Within each timestamp, run every tile through the model: its state is either kept in memory or restored from its checkpoint, as tile_state decides.
  4. Write the tile's requested native variables into the current timestamp's plane-oriented, little-endian output scratch file and, when the state is on disk, checkpoint its updated state.
  5. After all tiles complete that timestamp, resample its native variables onto each configured output grid, encode NETCDF, ZBIN, ZARR, PNGWJSON or GEOTIFF output, and remove the scratch file. Independent output variables may be postprocessed in parallel, and the whole step may run in the background while the next timestamp is stepped.
  6. Assemble any scheduled warm-state records in canonical model-cell order and write the configured legacy or NetCDF snapshot, in the same background step as the output.

Raster-backed models use clipped rectangular windows and omit empty windows. A window holding fewer than a quarter of a full tile's cells, as coastal and border windows do, is merged with a neighbour in its tile row, never beyond a full tile's worth of cells. Tiles are then ordered largest first so the work-stealing pool spends the tail of each timestep on the small ones. Models configured with legacy cell files use bounded batches in configured cell order. Both enter the same runner and model-adapter interface.

Meteorological input grids may be regular or curvilinear. Curvilinear grids retain nearest-neighbour R-tree lookup. Because source meteorological fields are normally low resolution, each decoded source field is cached whole and then sampled repeatedly for the model tiles.

GeoTIFF static layers and gridded warm-state variables are read using bounded source windows. The current configuration objects retain their compact active-cell properties and initial warm-state records; the warm state is released once every tile has been seeded from it. Exact per-tile live state, including transient accumulators and history, either stays in memory for the whole run or is checkpointed between timestamps, as tile_state decides. Decoded meteorological fields are retained while all tiles consume the current timestamp and then released. Scheduled warm-state records for the current timestamp are assembled in memory before the writer is called; native forecast output is the disk-backed portion of the pipeline.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The optional streaming section tunes the mandatory tiled runner:

streaming:
  tile_height: 1024
  tile_width: 1024
  cells_per_tile: 1048576
  max_memory: 6GB
  tile_state: auto
  overlap_postprocess: true
  scratch_directory: /var/tmp/risico

Defaults are 512 × 512 for raster tiles and 1,048,576 cells for legacy cell batches. scratch_directory defaults to a risico-streaming directory below the operating system's temporary directory. Tile dimensions and cells_per_tile must be greater than zero.

max_memory (for example 6GB or 768 MiB) is a target peak resident size. Tile concurrency is derived from what is left of it once the whole-domain arrays are charged, so the run adapts to the model and the domain; an explicit tile_concurrency wins over it. With neither set, one tile runs per core.

tile_state says where each tile's live state lives between timestamps:

  • auto (default): in memory when max_memory has room for every tile's state at the concurrency the run will use, or when no max_memory is set; on disk otherwise.
  • memory: always in memory. No checkpoint is written or read, which removes the largest I/O cost of a run.
  • disk: always checkpointed to the scratch directory, so only the tiles in flight hold state. This is the smallest footprint.

overlap_postprocess says whether a timestamp's output is resampled and written, and its warm state saved, while the next timestamp is being stepped. Unset, the overlap is taken when the output grids in flight and the gathered warm state still fit max_memory beside a step, or when no budget is set; true and false force it. At most one timestamp is finished in the background, so a failure there stops the run at the next timestamp.

Each model logs the decision it made and the peak it expects before the timeline starts, then logs per-timestamp phase timings (preload, step, postprocess, warm state) with the current and peak resident set size, and a total per phase at the end. streaming-inspect prints the same decision for a configuration without running it.

Output resolution does not affect numerical model execution: interpolation, clustering, precision rounding, and encoding happen only during the postprocessing stage.

See Configuration for the output formats.

NetCDF input files and warm-state snapshots are read with the pure-Rust netcdf-reader crate and snapshots are written with nc4-stream, so the build needs neither libnetcdf nor libhdf5.

Allow scratch capacity for approximately four bytes multiplied by active model cells and configured native variables, plus, when the state is on disk, the serialized live-state checkpoints and filesystem overhead. An output timestamp is held on disk only until it is postprocessed and removed; with overlap_postprocess that can be two timestamps at once.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Run a configuration directly with:

./target/release/risico-2023 \
  202607230000 \
  /share/risico/RISICO2023/configuration.yml \
  /path/to/generated-input-list.txt

The configured output and warm-state paths are live destinations. For development tests, copy the configuration and redirect those paths, plus streaming.scratch_directory, to a temporary directory.

docs.title: Inspecting a configuration
docs.text:
streaming-inspect builds each model, creates its tile plan, and instantiates the first tile's property/state adapters without running meteorological input or writing forecast output:

cargo run --bin streaming-inspect -- \
  202607240000 /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  --tile-height 256 --tile-width 256

The inspector still performs normal configuration and warm-state validation, so the referenced static layers, palettes, and required warm snapshot must exist.

docs.title: Failure and scratch behavior
docs.text: Model failures are logged independently so another configured model may continue. Completed output scratch files are removed after successful postprocessing. If execution is interrupted or fails before cleanup, the run-specific scratch directory may remain for diagnosis and can be removed after confirming that no process is using it.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Compile the production binary with Cargo. No native C libraries are needed: NetCDF and GeoTIFF I/O are pure Rust.

cargo build --release --bin risico-2023

The release workflow publishes a fully static x86_64-unknown-linux-musl binary that runs on any x86_64 Linux regardless of the glibc version. The same build works locally on Linux with the musl-tools package installed:

rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
cargo build --release --bin risico-2023 --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

./build-with-docker.sh still builds a glibc-linked binary inside an Ubuntu 16.04 container when one is needed.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
The executable takes a run date, a configuration file, and an input source:

./target/release/risico-2023 \
  YYYYMMDDHHMM \
  /path/to/configuration.yml \
  /path/to/input

The input source is either a directory containing NetCDF inputs or a text file listing legacy .zbin inputs.

docs.title: Try it with the sample data
docs.text:
The repository ships a small, ready-to-run case under docs/demo/data/: the static layers of a 1 km cut-out of the Italian domain around Liguria, one month of hourly weather (July 2025) as a NetCDF input on the same area, and a configuration that runs RISICO and FWI on them:

docs/demo/data/
├── static/                    domain mask, slope, aspect, vegetation id, PPF, vegetation catalogue
└── sample/
    ├── configuration.yml      RISICO (hourly) and FWI (daily), NetCDF outputs
    └── input/
        └── weather-2025-07.nc T, H, W, D, P, SNOW on a 0.125° grid, 744 hours

cargo build --release --bin risico-2023
cd docs/demo/data/sample
../../../../target/release/risico-2023 202507010000 configuration.yml input/

The run starts from default moisture (on_missing: defaults), takes about 20 seconds and writes one NetCDF file per variable under output/RISICO/ and output/FWI/, and the daily warm state under state/. Run it again with a later date, for example 202507150000, and each model starts from the warm state saved on that day. The same files are online: the weather input and the configuration.

The weather comes from the Open-Meteo historical forecast archive: weather data by Open-Meteo.com, licensed under CC BY 4.0; the file carries the same attribution in its attribution and license attributes. docs/demo/tools/make_sample_weather.py rebuilds it for any period.

docs.title: NetCDF inputs
docs.text:
Every .nc file in the input directory is inspected. By default a file provides latitude and longitude on two dimensions, a time axis and any of the input variables below, named as in the table (the names, the coordinate names and the time units can be remapped in the configuration). Files written on the same grid share one grid in memory; regular grids are mapped by their axes, curvilinear ones through an R-tree.

Variable Meaning Units T Forecast temperature °C or K K Observed temperature °C or K H Forecast relative humidity % F Observed relative humidity % R Dew point temperature °C or K Q, PSFC Specific humidity and surface pressure (to derive humidity) kg/kg, Pa W, D Wind speed and direction (from, meteorological) m/s, ° U, V Wind components m/s P Forecast precipitation mm O Observed precipitation mm SNOW Snow cover cm NDWI, NDVI, M, SWI Satellite indices –

docs.title: Development runs
docs.text:
The configured output and warm-state paths are live destinations. For development tests, copy the configuration and redirect those paths, plus streaming.scratch_directory, to a temporary directory.

Next: Configuration for static data, warm state and outputs, and Fire danger indices for the models a configuration can run.

docs.title: Fire Danger Indices
docs.text: One configuration can run any of the models below. Each is a models entry whose type selects the model; all share the input handler, the tiled runner and the output writers. The variable names in the tables are the internal_names an output type lists.

docs.title: RISICO
docs.text:
type: RISICO, model_version: legacy | v2023 | v2025. Static data: GeoTIFF domain mask, slope, aspect, vegetation id (with its catalogue) and, optionally, summer and winter PPF. Warm state: NetCDF snapshots.

RISICO follows the moisture of the dead fine fuel hour by hour, drying it with temperature, humidity and wind and wetting it with rain, and turns it into a rate of spread and a fireline intensity for the vegetation of each cell, corrected for wind and slope.

Variable Meaning Units dffm Dead fine fuel moisture % V Rate of spread m/h I Fireline intensity kW/m W Wind effect on spread – contrT Temperature effect on spread – VPPF, IPPF Spread and intensity weighted by the seasonal PPF layer m/h, kW/m NDVI, NDWI Satellite vegetation and water factors – VNDWI, INDWI, VNDVI, INDVI Spread and intensity with the satellite factors m/h, kW/m VPPFNDWI, IPPFNDWI, VPPFNDVI, IPPFNDVI Both PPF and satellite factors m/h, kW/m

The weather actually used is available as output too: temperature, humidity, windSpeed, windDir, rain and snowCover.

docs.title: Canadian Fire Weather Index System
docs.text:
type: FWI, model_version: legacy | cffdrs | sliding_window. Static data: a GeoTIFF domain mask. Warm state: NetCDF snapshots. See Configuration for the three versions.

Variable Meaning ffmc Fine Fuel Moisture Code dmc Duff Moisture Code dc Drought Code isi Initial Spread Index bui Build-Up Index fwi Fire Weather Index ifwi IFWI

docs.title: Cell-based indices
docs.text:
These models read their cells from a text file (cells_file_path), one lon lat value line per cell, where the third column is the mean annual rainfall (KBDI, Mark 5), the heat index (Orieux) or unused. Those with memory keep a text warm state (warm_state_path).

type Index Variables Warm state KBDI Keetch–Byram Drought Index kbdi (mm) yes Mark5 McArthur Forest Fire Danger Index, Mark 5 df drought factor, ffdi yes Angstrom Angström index angstrom no Fosberg Fosberg Fire Weather Index ffwi no Nesterov Nesterov ignition index nesterov yes Sharples Sharples fuel moisture and fire danger fmi, f no Orieux Orieux water reserve and danger class pet_t (mm), orieux_wr (mm), orieux_fd (0–3) yes Hdw Hot–Dry–Windy Index hdw no

The interactive demo runs all of them on one cell, side by side.

docs.title: Programmatic Workflow
docs.text: The models are a Rust library, risico, separate from the risico-2023 runner: every index is a pure computation on arrays of cells, with no files involved. Use it to embed RISICO in another program, run it on cells you already hold in memory, or test a formulation. This guide shows the model API; the full item-by-item documentation is in the API Reference.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
The library is published as the risico-2023 crate. Without the default build-binary feature it leaves out the runner's dependencies (NetCDF, GeoTIFF, Zarr, CLI):

[dependencies]
risico-2023 = { git = "https://github.com/CIMAFoundation/risico-2023", branch = "dev", default-features = false }
chrono = "0.4"

The crate is imported as risico. Add the config feature for the configuration.yml schema types (risico::config).

docs.title: The model API
docs.text:
Every model in risico::modules is made of the same pieces:

Piece Type What it holds Properties RISICOProperties, FWIProperties, ... What does not change during a run, one element per cell: coordinates, and for RISICO slope, aspect, vegetation and PPF Warm state RISICOWarmState, FWIWarmState, ... The per-cell memory a run starts from and saves at its end State RISICOState, FWIState, ... The running state, created from the warm state and a start time Input models::input::Input The weather of one timestamp on every cell Output models::output::Output The variables computed at one timestamp, read by OutputVariableName

Properties, states and inputs are aligned arrays: element i of each is the same cell.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
The library has its own units; the runner converts the input files to them:

Quantity Unit Temperature °C Relative humidity % Wind speed m/h Wind direction radians, the direction the wind comes from Rain mm Snow cover cm Slope, aspect radians

Missing values are risico::constants::NODATAVAL. InputElement::default() fills every field with it, so set the variables a model needs and leave the others.

docs.title: Stepping each model
docs.text:
The runner drives each model with the same calls in every tile; follow the same order:

Model Every timestamp When an output is wanted RISICO state.update(&props, &input) state.output(&props, &input) FWI state.update(&props, &input) state.output(&props) Mark 5 state.store(&input, &props) state.output(&props), once a day KBDI, Orieux state.store(&input) state.update(&props) then state.output(), once a day Nesterov state.store(&input, &props) state.update() then state.output(), once a day Angström, Fosberg, Sharples, HDW state.store(&input) state.output()

FWI steps at local standard noon: call FWIProperties::compute_standard_offsets once before the run.

docs.title: RISICO on one cell
docs.text:
examples/risico_single_cell.rs runs RISICO for two days of synthetic weather and prints the fine fuel moisture, rate of spread and intensity every six hours:

use std::{collections::HashMap, f32::consts::PI, sync::Arc};

use chrono::{Duration, TimeZone, Utc};
use risico::{
    models::{
        input::{Input, InputElement},
        output::OutputVariableName,
    },
    modules::risico::{
        config::RISICOModelConfig,
        models::{
            RISICOCellPropertiesContainer, RISICOProperties, RISICOState, RISICOVegetation,
            RISICOWarmState,
        },
    },
};

fn main() {
    // One cell: position, terrain and vegetation. The vegetation parameters
    // normally come from the catalogue CSV; the default is a generic fuel.
    let vegetation = Arc::new(RISICOVegetation::default());
    let properties = RISICOProperties::new(
        RISICOCellPropertiesContainer {
            lons: vec![8.86],
            lats: vec![44.45],
            slopes: vec![5.0_f32.to_radians()],
            aspects: vec![160.0_f32.to_radians()],
            vegetations: vec![vegetation.clone()],
        },
        HashMap::from([(vegetation.id.clone(), vegetation)]),
        vec![1.0], // summer PPF
        vec![1.0], // winter PPF
    );

    // Start from 40 % fine fuel moisture, the default warm state.
    let start = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();
    let mut state = RISICOState::new(&[RISICOWarmState::default()], &start, RISICOModelConfig::new("v2025"));

    for hour in 1..=48 {
        let time = start + Duration::hours(hour);
        let phase = 2.0 * PI * ((hour as f32 - 15.0) / 24.0);
        // Units are the library's own: wind speed in m/h, direction in radians.
        let weather = InputElement {
            temperature: 26.0 + 6.0 * phase.cos(),
            humidity: 45.0 - 20.0 * phase.cos(),
            wind_speed: 4.0 * 3600.0,
            wind_dir: 270.0_f32.to_radians(),
            rain: 0.0,
            snow_cover: 0.0,
            ..InputElement::default()
        };
        let input = Input { time, data: vec![weather].into() };

        state.update(&properties, &input);
        if hour % 6 == 0 {
            let output = state.output(&properties, &input);
            let value = |name| output.get(&name).unwrap()[0];
            println!(
                "{time}  dffm {:5.1} %  V {:6.1} m/h  I {:7.1} kW/m",
                value(OutputVariableName::dffm),
                value(OutputVariableName::V),
                value(OutputVariableName::I),
            );
        }
    }
}

$ cargo run --release --example risico_single_cell
2026-07-01 06:00:00 UTC  dffm  35.7 %  V    7.1 m/h  I    10.6 kW/m
2026-07-01 12:00:00 UTC  dffm  30.8 %  V   17.7 m/h  I    28.7 kW/m
2026-07-01 18:00:00 UTC  dffm  25.7 %  V   41.4 m/h  I    73.3 kW/m
...
2026-07-03 00:00:00 UTC  dffm  12.7 %  V  139.6 m/h  I   298.9 kW/m

RISICOModelConfig::new selects the formulation: legacy, v2023 or v2025.

docs.title: Vegetation
docs.text:
RISICOVegetation holds one row of the vegetation catalogue (p_vegetazione.csv):

Field Meaning id, name Identifier in the vegetation-id layer, description d0, d1 Dead fine fuel load, live fuel load hhv Higher heating value [kJ/kg] umid Live fuel moisture v0 Base rate of spread [m/h] T0 Response time of the dead fine fuel moisture [h] sat Saturation moisture of the dead fine fuel [%] use_ndvi Whether satellite NDVI modulates the live fuel

docs.title: FWI on one cell
docs.text:
examples/fwi_single_cell.rs runs the Canadian FWI System for five days of hourly weather and prints the codes at noon:

use chrono::{Duration, TimeZone, Utc};
use risico::{
    models::{
        input::{Input, InputElement},
        output::OutputVariableName,
    },
    modules::fwi::{
        config::FWIModelConfig,
        models::{FWICellPropertiesContainer, FWIProperties, FWIState, FWIWarmState},
    },
};

fn main() {
    let start = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();

    let mut properties = FWIProperties::new(FWICellPropertiesContainer {
        lons: vec![8.86],
        lats: vec![44.45],
    });
    // FWI steps at local standard noon: resolve each cell's UTC offset once.
    properties.compute_standard_offsets(&start);

    // A warm state is a short history of codes; start from the standard
    // FFMC 85, DMC 6, DC 15 the day before.
    let warm_state = FWIWarmState {
        dates: vec![start - Duration::days(1)],
        ffmc: vec![85.0],
        dmc: vec![6.0],
        dc: vec![15.0],
        rain: vec![0.0],
    };
    let mut state = FWIState::new(&[warm_state], &start, FWIModelConfig::new("legacy"));

    for hour in 1..=5 * 24 {
        let time = start + Duration::hours(hour);
        let weather = InputElement {
            temperature: 28.0,
            humidity: 30.0,
            wind_speed: 5.0 * 3600.0, // m/h
            rain: 0.0,
            ..InputElement::default()
        };
        state.update(&properties, &Input { time, data: vec![weather].into() });

        if hour % 24 == 12 {
            let output = state.output(&properties);
            let value = |name| output.get(&name).unwrap()[0];
            println!(
                "{time}  FFMC {:5.1}  DMC {:5.1}  DC {:6.1}  ISI {:4.1}  BUI {:5.1}  FWI {:4.1}",
                value(OutputVariableName::ffmc),
                value(OutputVariableName::dmc),
                value(OutputVariableName::dc),
                value(OutputVariableName::isi),
                value(OutputVariableName::bui),
                value(OutputVariableName::fwi),
            );
        }
    }
}

$ cargo run --release --example fwi_single_cell
2026-07-01 12:00:00 UTC  FFMC  91.8  DMC  10.8  DC   23.7  ISI 13.8  BUI  10.7  FWI 13.5
2026-07-02 12:00:00 UTC  FFMC  92.4  DMC  15.6  DC   32.5  ISI 15.0  BUI  15.5  FWI 17.0
...
2026-07-05 12:00:00 UTC  FFMC  92.6  DMC  29.9  DC   58.7  ISI 15.3  BUI  29.8  FWI 23.3

docs.title: Many cells
docs.text:
Nothing changes for a grid: pass one element per cell in every vector, and one InputElement per cell in each Input. update and output process the cells in parallel with ndarray's Zip. The risico-2023 runner does exactly this on tiles of the domain, so memory stays bounded however large the domain is (see Tiled Streaming Execution).

To save and restore a run, map the state's cells back to warm-state records (for RISICO, the dffm, snow and satellite fields of each RISICOStateElement) and pass them to State::new next time.

docs.title: Building the Web Demo
docs.text:
The interactive demo runs the unmodified risico-2023 binary, compiled for the WASI target:

rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 --bin risico-2023
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/risico-2023.wasm docs/demo/

The docs workflow does the same on every push to dev and main, so the bundle is never committed.

docs.title: What differs on WASI
docs.text:
The WASI build is the same program with a few platform switches:

  • Zarr output is not available: zarrs and its zstd dependency do not build for WASI. The demo writes NetCDF only.
  • NetCDF files are read into memory where the reader has no positioned file access (open_netcdf in src/bin/common/io/mod.rs).
  • No threads: there is no tile pool and rayon runs on the calling thread.
  • The temporary directory is $TMPDIR (or /tmp) and the process id is 0.

docs.title: How the page runs it
docs.text:
docs/demo/ holds a static page and a few ES modules:

File Role app.html, app.js The page: map, controls, charts, map rendering worker.js Runs the binary in a Web Worker lib/runner.js Builds an in-memory filesystem with @bjorn3/browser_wasi_shim, runs the binary, collects its files lib/scenario.js Turns a scenario into configuration.yml, static layers, cell lists and arguments lib/netcdf3.js Writes the weather input as a NetCDF classic file lib/geotiff-write.js Writes the domain mask and static layers as GeoTIFFs lib/openmeteo.js Fetches hourly weather from Open-Meteo

The outputs are the binary's own NetCDF-4 files, read with h5wasm. The shim grows a file by reallocating it on every write; runner.js replaces that with a doubling buffer, which cut the time spent writing outputs by a factor of five on a run over the whole of Italy.

The static layers the page loads (docs/demo/data/static/) are a cut-out of the 1 km Italian domain around Liguria (7.40–10.20 °E, 43.70–44.75 °N, 274 × 103 cells): domain mask, slope, aspect, vegetation id, PPF and the vegetation catalogue, plus the colour palettes in docs/demo/data/palettes/. docs/demo/data/sample/ holds the July 2025 weather the page uses by default (a NetCDF input, rebuilt by docs/demo/tools/make_sample_weather.py) and a configuration to run it with the command-line model. The page reads whatever grid the layers define, so a larger domain only needs other files; for one the size of Italy (317 000 cells) set a coarser Open-Meteo grid (COARSE, REFINE in app.js) and expect about a minute and 1.1 GB of browser memory.

docs.title: Testing locally
docs.text:
Serve docs/ with any static server that sends application/wasm for .wasm files:

python3 -m http.server --directory docs 8765

and open http://127.0.0.1:8765/demo/app.html. mkdocs serve works too and shows the page inside the documentation.
